---
title: "Matrix Decompositions — Build Big Work From Simple Pieces"
description: "A compact linear-algebra lesson with mathematical definitions, real values and reasoning."
---

## Start with a question

Instead of solving a brand-new system from scratch every time, can a matrix be split into reusable simpler pieces?

## Understand the central idea

One common decomposition is LU: a lower-triangular matrix followed by an upper-triangular one. This separates a system into two easier triangular solves.

## Express it with mathematics

$$
A=LU,\qquad \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\4&3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\2&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\0&1\end{bmatrix}
$$

**Every symbol explained:** A is the original matrix; L is lower triangular (zeros above the diagonal) and U is upper triangular (zeros below the diagonal). Multiplication LU reconstructs A.

**Substitute real numbers:** Multiply first row of L by U: [2,1]. Multiply second row: 2×[2,1]+[0,1]=[4,3]. Thus the product really is [[2,1],[4,3]].

## Why this works

For Ax=b, first solve Ly=b for the intermediate y, then Ux=y. Triangular solves are simpler than unconstrained dense systems and can reuse factors for multiple right-hand sides.

## What can go wrong?

Not every matrix admits this exact LU form without row permutation; robust implementations commonly use PA=LU, where P records pivoting. Also explain QR and SVD separately when a task requires them.

## Your turn

For b=(3,7), solve Ly=b, then Ux=y. Check by multiplying Ax.
